analysis.one_liner: Requires beef processors to test for E. coli and lets USDA trace contaminated ground beef to its source.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it sat in the House Agriculture Committee after referral in July 2010, was sent to a subcommittee that November, and died when the 111th Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have amended federal meat inspection law to require beef slaughterhouses, processing plants, and grinding facilities to test for a dangerous strain of E. coli in beef trimmings and ground beef, report positive results to USDA within 24 hours, and trace contamination back to its original source. It also would have applied the same testing rules to imported beef, publicly listed repeat violators, and given small facilities grants of up to $10,000 to help comply. The bill was referred to the House Agriculture Committee and never received a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers of ground beef, which is nearly everyone: the bill would have required testing at every stage of beef trim production and grinding, traced contaminated meat to its source, banned imports that fail to meet the same testing standard, and publicly identified plants with repeated contamination. Children, the elderly, and people with weakened immune systems — those most likely to die or suffer kidney failure from E. coli — benefit most. Small slaughterhouses and grinding facilities would also receive federal grants of up to $10,000 to help them comply.

how_it_helps.text: It requires slaughterhouses, processing plants, and grinding facilities to test each lot of beef trimmings and ground beef for Shiga toxin-producing E. coli and report positive results to the USDA within 24 hours.

When a sample tests positive, USDA must trace the contamination back to the original source—slaughterhouse, packer, or processor—and the contaminated lot must be destroyed or treated before it can be sold.
Ground beef imported from other countries would face the same testing requirements as domestic beef, closing a gap in current coverage.
Testing would be done by independent accredited labs, and a facility could not fire its lab for reporting positive results—an anti-interference safeguard.
Plants with repeated positive tests would be publicly listed as 'habitual violators' on a USDA website.

analysis.who_pays: Meatpacking companies and beef processing plants, which would bear the cost of mandatory testing, independent lab contracts, 24-hour reporting, trace-back investigations, corrective action, and public listing for repeat violations. Foreign beef suppliers would face the same testing requirements on imports. Small facilities would get grants to offset compliance costs.

drawbacks.text: Mandatory E. coli testing at every lot, independent lab contracts, and trace-back investigations would impose significant compliance costs on slaughterhouses and grinding facilities, and those costs could partly be passed to consumers through beef prices.

Plants with repeated positive tests would be publicly listed as 'habitual violators,' which critics could view as punitive publicity based on testing results that can vary; and daily sampling for 15 consecutive days after any positive result is a heavy burden for a facility.

USDA already tests beef for E. coli under its existing inspection authority, so supporters of the status quo would argue the bill duplicates existing Food Safety and Inspection Service programs rather than adding new protection.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit—fewer E. coli poisonings from ground beef—would have come at a real cost to meat processors, who would bear testing and possible disposal expenses, though USDA grants cushioned the smallest facilities and the compliance deadlines phased in over three years. The bill was phased so that the largest plants were covered first. The main drawback is that the testing and traceability rules would add cost and paperwork throughout the beef supply chain, some of which might reach consumers in prices; the strongest good-faith objection is that FSIS's existing testing and recall system already addresses E. coli. On balance, this was a public-health bill whose costs fell mostly on the industry responsible for contamination.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Agriculture Committee on the day it was introduced, later sent to its Livestock, Dairy, and Poultry subcommittee, and was never reported out or brought to a vote before the 111th Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Rosa DeLauro introduced H.R. 6024 on July 30, 2010 with seven cosponsors, all Democrats.
The House referred the bill to the Agriculture Committee the same day; it never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote in the record.
On November 16, 2010, the bill was referred to the Subcommittee on Livestock, Dairy, and Poultry—a step that often signals a bill is not moving.
The 111th Congress ended January 3, 2011, and the bill died with it, having never gotten a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Beef slaughterhouses, processors, and grinding facilities are better off: they avoid the testing, trace-back, and public-listing requirements the bill would have imposed. Importers of foreign beef trim also avoid the added verification costs.

for.name: Rosa DeLauro
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on July 30, 2010 to mandate E. coli testing, trace-back, and public listing of repeat violators in the beef industry.

for.name: 7 of 253 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction: Schakowsky, McDermott, Lowey, Grijalva, Lee of California, Meeks of New York, and Richardson.

against.name: House Agriculture Committee (111th Congress)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day of introduction and never reported it out or acted on it beyond sending it to subcommittee.

against.name: Subcommittee on Livestock, Dairy, and Poultry
against.what_they_did: Took referral of the bill on November 16, 2010, and took no further action on it in the record.

against.name: Meat and beef processing industry
against.what_they_did: The beef and meatpacking industry has historically opposed mandatory testing and trace-back requirements that add compliance costs, though no industry action on this specific bill appears in the congressional record.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's support was entirely Democratic — the sponsor and all seven cosponsors were House Democrats — and it received no recorded Republican support before dying in committee.

industries.note: The bill would require them to test every lot of trim and ground beef, use independent accredited labs, report positive results within 24 hours, and face trace-backs and public 'habitual violator' listing. They bear the compliance cost; the public gains safer ground beef.

industries.industry: Beef importers and foreign beef suppliers
industries.note: Imported trim and ground beef would have to meet the same testing requirements as domestic beef, with certification and secondary testing at the domestic facility. This removes a cost advantage of foreign sourcing.
Every covered facility would have to contract annually with an accredited independent lab, and labs would need proficiency-verification services, creating steady demand for testing services.
